# How to Reduce AI API Latency: 7 Proven Techniques
## 1. Stream Your Responses
Instead of waiting for the entire response to generate, stream tokens as they arrive.

## 2. Enable Prompt Caching
If your requests share a common system prompt or context block, prompt caching avoids re-processing those tokens on every call. Anthropic's prompt caching stores the KV-cache of your prefix, so subsequent requests with the same prefix skip the prefill phase entirely.

python Copy

The numbers are significant: for a 4,000-token system prompt, cached requests see TTFT drop from ~800ms to ~300ms. You also save 90% on those cached input tokens. Read more in our prompt caching deep dive.

## 3. Trim Your Input Tokens
Streaming and prompt caching deliver the biggest wins with the least effort — start there

## Putting It All Together
1. **Always stream.** Takes 2 lines of code, cuts perceived latency by 90%.
2. **Cache your system prompt.** Add `cache_control` to your system message. Done.

web.title: TLDR
web.description:
## TLDR

Problem this solves:

- OpenAI-shaped streams send zero bytes until the first model token
- Ingresses and load balancers kill those silent connections at their idle timeout
- Keepalive pings today require per-deployment `keepalive_seconds` opt-in

How it solves it:

- Adds global `litellm_settings.sse_keepalive_ping_interval_seconds`
- Used when neither the request nor the deployment sets an interval
- A deployment's explicit `keepalive_seconds: 0` disable still wins
- Also arms keepalive on router-less proxies

## User Flow

Before: a developer streaming a long document to their self-hosted model through the company ingress gets a 504 before the first token ever arrives

1. They send POST [https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions](https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions) with `"model": "qwen-local"`, `"stream": true`, and a ~16k-token document prompt
2. The self-hosted backend starts crunching the prompt; the first token is about 2.5 minutes away and the connection carries zero bytes in the meantime
3. At exactly 60 seconds the ingress gives up on the silent connection and returns `504 Gateway Time-out`; no SSE data ever arrives
4. Every retry dies the same way, so requests past the ingress idle timeout can never complete

After: the same request emits `: ping` comments within seconds, holds the connection open through the whole prompt crunch, and completes

1. The proxy admin sets `litellm_settings.sse_keepalive_ping_interval_seconds: 3` and restarts the gateway
2. The developer sends the same POST [https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions](https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions) with the same document prompt
3. Within ~3 seconds a `200` with `Content-Type: text/event-stream` arrives, followed by a `: ping` comment every 3 seconds
4. About 2.5 minutes in the real `data:` chunks arrive, then `data: [DONE]`; SSE-conformant clients ignore the comment lines, so nothing else about the stream changes

web.description:
# Add streaming to your LLM app the simple way
## When to use which
- **SSE:** chat responses, summaries, code gen, anything read‑only to the browser.
- **Mix:** start with SSE; add WS later for the few places that need it. Streaming tokens are temporary, unique credentials used by online video platforms to authenticate and authorize a user's access to a specific video stream.

## Gateways and proxies (avoid buffering surprises)
- Use **HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2** with keep‑alive; avoid intermediaries that coalesce chunks.
- Send **Content-Type: text/event-stream** for SSE with Cache-Control: no-store and Connection: keep-alive.

## UX tips that make streaming feel fast
- Keep system prompts short; tight output caps stop rambling.
- Log the **first token timestamp** to spot regressions.

## Token streaming that feels fast and costs less
Use SSE for most chat. Cancel promptly, cap outputs, and turn off proxy buffering.

web.title: maxeaglet/commandcode-proxy
web.description:
# Command Code Proxy
## API Endpoints
### `POST /v1/responses`
- **First-token silence and keep-alive**: `response.created` / `response.in_progress` are emitted **immediately** once upstream returns `200`, and a `: keepalive` SSE comment follows every 5 s while waiting. Time-to-first-token for a reasoning model with a large prompt measured 15–40 s; that silent window used to put **zero bytes** on the wire, so intermediate layers (EdgeOne's origin idle timeout measured ~15 s) or client first-byte timeouts cut the connection — visible as nginx `499` with `body_bytes_sent=0` and a client retrying every 15 s. SSE comments must be ignored by clients per spec (`/v1/messages` uses `event: ping`, but Responses has no ping event and an unknown event type risks strict-parser errors).

web.title: Serve a useChat frontend from Go
web.description:
## Keep-alive

Coding agents and slow tools can leave a stream quiet for a minute. Idle connections get closed by proxies and load balancers. `UIMessageStreamResponseInit.KeepAliveMs` makes the pipe send an opening `: stream-open` comment right away, then a `: keep-alive` comment whenever the stream has been silent for that long. SSE clients ignore comments.

```go
keepAlive := 15 * time.Second
err := ai.PipeUIMessageChunksToResponse(chunks, w, &ai.UIMessageStreamResponseInit{
	KeepAliveMs: &keepAlive,
})
```

The field is a `*time.Duration`, despite the `Ms` suffix, which it keeps for parity with the TypeScript option. Pick an interval shorter than your proxy's idle timeout.

## CORS

When the frontend and the API live on different origins, such as `localhost:3000` and `localhost:8080`, the browser sends a preflight `OPTIONS` request because the body is JSON. Answer it, and name the one origin you trust:

```go
func withCORS(origin string, next http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		w.Header().Set("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", origin)
		w.Header().Set("Access-Control-Allow-Headers", "Content-Type")
		w.Header().Set("Access-Control-Allow-Methods", "GET, POST, OPTIONS")
		if r.Method == http.MethodOptions {
			w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
			return
		}
		next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
	})
}
```

If you send an `Authorization` header from the client, add it to `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`. If you serve the frontend and the API from one origin, or proxy `/api` through your frontend server, you do not need CORS.

## Proxies and buffering

SSE only works if every layer between Go and the browser passes bytes through as they arrive. The SDK flushes after every chunk and sends `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `X-Accel-Buffering: no`. The rest is up to your stack:

- **Wrap the `ResponseWriter` carefully.** Logging, metrics and compression middleware often wrap the writer in a type that does not implement `http.Flusher`. The SDK then cannot flush, and the output arrives in large blocks. Implement `Flush` on your wrapper by delegating to the underlying writer, or skip the wrapper for this route.

web.description:
# 🚀 PromptCache
### Reduce LLM cost and latency with semantic caching
It adds Bearer-token authentication for management endpoints, SSE streaming support, runtime threshold configuration, and cache warming.

## Streaming
- On a cache miss, PromptCache forwards the provider stream and buffers the assembled response for caching.
- On a cache hit, it synthesizes OpenAI-compatible SSE chunks from the cached response.
